bio.topic: Limiting factors of photosynthesis and investigations

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: State the term for the factor that is in shortest supply and therefore restricts the rate of photosynthesis.
questions.hint: It 'limits' the rate.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Which of these is NOT usually a limiting factor of photosynthesis?
questions.hint: Think about which substances are reactants or affect enzymes.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: In a pondweed experiment, what is usually counted to measure the rate of photosynthesis?
questions.hint: Which product is a gas?

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: A lamp is moved closer to a pondweed. What is the independent variable?
questions.hint: The independent variable is the one you change.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Why is a beaker of water often placed between the lamp and the pondweed?
options: To absorb heat so temperature stays constant
questions.answer: To absorb heat so temperature stays constant
questions.hint: Lamps give out more than light.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Sodium hydrogencarbonate is added to the water around pondweed. What does it provide?

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: On a graph of rate against light intensity, the line rises and then levels off. What does the levelling off show?
questions.hint: Adding more light no longer increases the rate.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Above about 40 °C, the rate of photosynthesis falls sharply. Why?

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: What is the colour of hydrogencarbonate indicator in air with normal (atmospheric) carbon dioxide concentration?
questions.hint: It is between the high-CO₂ and low-CO₂ colours.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Hydrogencarbonate indicator turns purple. What does this show about the carbon dioxide concentration?

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: A leaf is sealed in a tube of hydrogencarbonate indicator and kept in the dark. What colour will the indicator turn?
questions.hint: In the dark the leaf can respire but cannot photosynthesise.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: A tube with indicator but no leaf is set up alongside the others. What is its purpose?

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: A pondweed produced 36 bubbles in 3 minutes. Calculate the rate of photosynthesis in bubbles per minute.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the lamp. If the distance is doubled, the light intensity becomes…
questions.hint: Use 1/d².

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Why do some greenhouse growers burn paraffin heaters in winter?
options: To increase both temperature and carbon dioxide
questions.answer: To increase both temperature and carbon dioxide
questions.hint: Think about the products of combustion.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Explain why counting bubbles is a less accurate method than collecting the gas in a measuring cylinder or gas syringe, and suggest one other way to improve the reliability of the investigation.
questions.hint: Think about bubble size and repeats.

bss.topic: Abertura política, Anistia e Diretas Já

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Como ficou conhecido o projeto do governo militar, iniciado em 1974, de devolver o poder aos civis aos poucos?

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Em que ano foi aprovada a Lei da Anistia no Brasil?

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual era o slogan dos movimentos que pediam uma anistia sem restrições? Anistia ampla, geral e ___.
questions.hint: Significa 'sem restrições'.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual Ato Institucional, considerado o mais duro da ditadura, deixou de valer no início de 1979?

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Quem foram beneficiados pela Lei da Anistia de 1979?
options: Opositores e também agentes do Estado acusados de crimes
questions.answer: Opositores e também agentes do Estado acusados de crimes
questions.hint: A lei foi chamada de 'recíproca'.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual foi uma consequência direta da anistia de 1979?
options: O retorno de exilados ao Brasil
O fim imediato do governo militar
questions.answer: O retorno de exilados ao Brasil

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Em 1979, a reforma partidária acabou com qual sistema?

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Em 1982, os brasileiros voltaram a votar diretamente para qual cargo?

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual movimento popular de 1983–1984 pedia eleições diretas para presidente?

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: O que propunha a emenda constitucional defendida pelo movimento Diretas Já?

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: O que aconteceu com essa emenda na votação de abril de 1984?
options: Foi rejeitada por não alcançar votos suficientes
questions.answer: Foi rejeitada por não alcançar votos suficientes
questions.hint: Ela precisava de dois terços da Câmara.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Como foi escolhido o primeiro presidente civil, em 1985?
options: Pelo Colégio Eleitoral, de forma indireta
questions.answer: Pelo Colégio Eleitoral, de forma indireta

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual palavra designa o processo de volta à democracia no Brasil nos anos 1980?

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual documento, promulgado em 1988, marcou juridicamente o fim da transição?

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Explique por que a abertura política foi chamada de 'lenta e gradual' e por que os militares preferiram controlar o ritmo da transição.
questions.hint: Pense em quem queria evitar mudanças bruscas e por quê.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Analise por que a Lei da Anistia de 1979 é até hoje debatida no Brasil, considerando quem foi beneficiado por ela.
questions.hint: Compare a anistia pedida pelos movimentos com a lei aprovada.

bus.topic: Financial and non-financial methods of motivation

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A worker is paid £12 for every hour worked. This is an example of…

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A fixed annual amount paid in equal monthly instalments is called…

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: What is the term for payment based on a percentage of the value of sales made?
questions.hint: Common for sales staff.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which of these is a financial method of motivation?

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which is a non-financial method of motivation?

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: What term describes workers moving between different tasks at the same skill level?

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Giving workers more tasks of a similar level of difficulty is called…
questions.hint: Think of 'larger' job, not 'richer'.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Giving workers more challenging tasks and responsibility is called…

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A salesperson earns a basic salary of $1,500 a month plus 5% commission. In one month she sells $20,000 of goods. Calculate her total pay in dollars.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A worker earns £14 per hour and works 38 hours a week. Calculate the weekly wage in pounds.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: One disadvantage of commission for a business is that…
options: staff may pressure customers into buying
it is hard to calculate pay
it removes the incentive to sell
questions.answer: staff may pressure customers into buying

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which method is most likely to suit a production line worker doing repetitive tasks?
questions.hint: Which reduces boredom?

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Organising workers into groups responsible for a whole section of work is called…

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A disadvantage of job rotation for a business is that…

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of paying a bonus to factory workers.
questions.hint: Think about output and quality.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A clothing shop wants to motivate its sales assistants. Evaluate whether commission or job enrichment would be the better method. Justify your answer.
questions.hint: Consider cost, behaviour with customers and long-term motivation.

chem.topic: Electrolysis of molten compounds and aqueous solutions

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: What is electrolysis?
options: The breakdown of an ionic compound using electricity
The dissolving of a salt in water
The reaction of an acid with a base
questions.answer: The breakdown of an ionic compound using electricity

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: What name is given to the liquid or solution that conducts electricity and is broken down in electrolysis?

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Which electrode is negative?
questions.hint: Positive ions move towards it.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Why must an ionic compound be molten or dissolved to be electrolysed?
options: So the ions are free to move
So electrons can move through the solid
questions.answer: So the ions are free to move

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Why are graphite or platinum used as electrodes?
options: They are inert and conduct electricity
questions.answer: They are inert and conduct electricity

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed. What forms at the cathode?

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed. What is seen at the anode?
questions.hint: Think about what bromine looks like.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Which half-equation shows the reaction at the cathode for molten sodium chloride?
questions.hint: Reduction is gain of electrons.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: In aqueous solutions, hydrogen is produced at the cathode if the metal is…

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride (brine) is electrolysed. What forms at the anode?

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Brine is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What forms at the cathode?

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Name the solution left behind after the electrolysis of brine.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed with graphite electrodes. What forms at the cathode?

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed with graphite electrodes. What forms at the anode?
questions.hint: Sulfate ions are not discharged.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: During electrolysis of copper(II) sulfate with graphite electrodes, the blue colour of the solution…
questions.hint: Copper ions are being removed.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Copper(II) sulfate solution is electrolysed using copper electrodes. Describe and explain what happens to the mass of each electrode.
questions.hint: Think about which electrode loses copper ions and which gains copper atoms.

comp.topic: Computer architecture: CPU, von Neumann model and fetch–decode–execute cycle

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: What does CPU stand for?
questions.hint: Think about what the CPU does: it processes data at the centre of the computer.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which component of the CPU carries out arithmetic and logical operations?
questions.hint: Its name includes the words 'arithmetic' and 'logic'.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which component of the CPU decodes instructions and sends control signals to other components?
questions.hint: It coordinates and directs what the other parts do.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: In the von Neumann model, data and instructions are stored together in the same ___. (one word)
questions.hint: Think about where programs are held while they run.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which register holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched?
questions.hint: This register 'counts' through the program.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which register holds the address of the memory location currently being read from or written to?
questions.hint: Look for the register with 'address' in its name that connects to memory.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which register temporarily stores the data or instruction that has just been fetched from memory?
questions.hint: Its name refers to the data travelling to or from memory.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which register stores the results of calculations carried out by the ALU?
questions.hint: It 'accumulates' results.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which bus is unidirectional, carrying signals only from the CPU to memory?
questions.hint: The CPU tells memory where to look, but memory never sends a location back.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which bus carries signals such as 'memory read' and 'memory write'?
questions.hint: These signals control what happens, rather than carrying data or locations.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Name the three stages of the cycle the CPU repeats to run a program, in order, separated by dashes.
questions.hint: The first stage gets the instruction from memory.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: During the fetch stage, what happens immediately after the address in the PC is copied to the MAR?
options: The instruction is executed by the ALU
The result is stored in the ACC
The control unit decodes the instruction
questions.hint: The PC must be ready to point to the following instruction.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which statement about the data bus is correct?
options: It only carries signals from memory to the CPU
It connects the PC directly to the ALU
questions.hint: Data needs to travel both to and from memory.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: A CPU has a 16-bit address bus. How many different memory locations can it address? Give the number in full.
questions.hint: Each extra address line doubles the number of locations: work out 2 to the power of the number of lines.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Describe what happens during the fetch stage of the fetch–decode–execute cycle. Refer to the registers and buses involved.
questions.hint: Mention the PC, MAR, address bus, data bus, MDR and CIR in the order they are used.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Explain why the von Neumann model is described as a 'stored program' concept, and give one limitation of using a single bus for both data and instructions.
questions.hint: Think about where the program lives and what happens when data and instructions need to travel at the same time.

econ.topic: The mixed economic system and government intervention in markets

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: What is a mixed economy?
options: An economy where resources are allocated by both the private sector and the government
An economy where the government owns all resources
An economy with no government involvement
An economy that only trades with other countries
questions.answer: An economy where resources are allocated by both the private sector and the government
questions.hint: Think about which two sectors are 'mixed'.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: A maximum price is set ___ the equilibrium price in order to have an effect.
questions.hint: A price ceiling is meant to make a product cheaper.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: What is the most likely result of an effective maximum price?
questions.hint: At a lower price, compare how much people want to buy with how much firms want to sell.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: A minimum wage is an example of which type of government intervention?
questions.hint: It sets a floor below which the price of labour cannot fall.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: What is the most likely result of a minimum price set above equilibrium?
questions.hint: At a higher price, producers want to sell more but consumers want to buy less.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: A tax on spending, such as a tax on cigarettes, is called an ___ tax. (one word)
questions.hint: It is paid to the government through the seller, not directly from income.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: What happens to the supply curve when the government places an indirect tax on a product?
questions.hint: A tax raises firms' costs of production.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: A payment from the government to producers to lower their costs and encourage output is called a ___. (one word)
questions.hint: It is the opposite of a tax on production.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: What happens to the equilibrium price and quantity when a subsidy is given to producers?
questions.hint: The subsidy shifts supply to the right.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: The transfer of a firm from the public sector to the private sector is called ___.
questions.hint: The firm becomes 'private'.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: The transfer of a firm from the private sector to the public sector is called ___.
questions.hint: The firm becomes owned by the nation.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Which of the following is an example of regulation?
options: A law banning the sale of alcohol to under-18s
questions.answer: A law banning the sale of alcohol to under-18s
questions.hint: Regulation uses rules and laws rather than money.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: The government places a tax of $2 per unit on a good. The price paid by consumers rises from $10 to $11.50. How much of the tax is paid by consumers per unit?
questions.hint: Compare the old and new prices paid by consumers.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Explain two reasons why a government might subsidise public transport.
questions.hint: Think about external benefits, such as less pollution and congestion, and about helping people on low incomes.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Analyse why a maximum price on rented housing might lead to a shortage of homes to rent.
questions.hint: Use demand and supply: what happens to the quantity landlords want to supply and the quantity tenants demand at the lower price?

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Discuss whether privatisation of a state-owned water company is likely to benefit consumers.
questions.hint: Consider efficiency and investment on one side, and higher prices or a private monopoly on the other, then reach a judgement.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What is the main purpose of a summary?
options: To give the key points of a text briefly in your own words
To copy the most interesting sentences
To give your opinion on the text
To add new information to the text
questions.answer: To give the key points of a text briefly in your own words
questions.hint: A summary is shorter than the original and focuses on the main ideas.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Before choosing points for a summary, what should you check first?
questions.hint: Only points that match what the question asks for will gain marks.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: A summary task asks for 'the benefits of urban gardens'. Which point is relevant?
options: Urban gardens give residents fresh vegetables
Urban gardens were first recorded long ago
The writer visited a garden last summer
questions.answer: Urban gardens give residents fresh vegetables
questions.hint: Look for a point that is a benefit.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: A summary task asks for 'the difficulties of living in space'. Which point is NOT relevant?
options: Astronauts can see beautiful views of Earth
Astronauts are far from their families
questions.answer: Astronauts can see beautiful views of Earth
questions.hint: Which option is a positive rather than a difficulty?

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which of these should you leave out of a summary?
questions.hint: A summary keeps only what is essential.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Why should you use your own words in a summary where possible?
options: To show you understand the text
questions.answer: To show you understand the text
questions.hint: Copying long phrases does not prove understanding.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which is the best way to organise points in a summary?
options: Group similar points together in a logical order
questions.answer: Group similar points together in a logical order
questions.hint: A reader should be able to follow the ideas smoothly.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which connective best links two similar points in a summary?
questions.hint: You need a word that adds another point, not one that contrasts.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which connective best introduces a contrasting point?
questions.hint: You need a word that shows a change of direction.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Original: 'The trip was ruined by heavy rain, freezing wind and a broken-down coach.' Which is the best concise summary point?
options: Bad weather and transport problems spoiled the trip
The trip was ruined by heavy rain, freezing wind and a broken-down coach
The coach was old and needed new tyres
questions.answer: Bad weather and transport problems spoiled the trip
questions.hint: Look for an option that groups the details into general ideas without copying.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Grouping 'apples, oranges and bananas' as 'fruit' is an example of which summary skill?
questions.hint: You replace a list of specific items with one general term.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: A text says: 'Scientists warn that, although plastic is cheap, it lasts for centuries and harms sea life.' If the summary focus is 'problems with plastic', which part is relevant?
options: It lasts for centuries and harms sea life
questions.answer: It lasts for centuries and harms sea life
questions.hint: 'Cheap' is an advantage, not a problem.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which of these is a common mistake in summary writing?
questions.hint: A summary reports the text's ideas, not yours.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What should you do if your summary is over the word limit?
options: Remove less important details and combine points
questions.answer: Remove less important details and combine points
questions.hint: Think about which details are not essential to the focus.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Explain how you would identify relevant points in a long article before writing a summary.
questions.hint: Think about re-reading the question, underlining, and checking each point against the focus.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Explain why organising points logically makes a summary more effective for the reader.
questions.hint: Consider clarity, flow and how easily the reader can follow the ideas.

en_lit.topic: Drama: conventions — stage directions, dialogue and dramatic irony

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What are stage directions?
options: Instructions in a script about actions, setting or how lines are spoken
The list of characters at the start
questions.answer: Instructions in a script about actions, setting or how lines are spoken
questions.hint: They tell actors and directors what to do, not what to say.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: How are stage directions usually set out in a printed play?
questions.hint: They need to look different from the spoken lines.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What term is used for a conversation between two or more characters in a play?
questions.hint: It comes from a Greek word meaning 'conversation'.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What is dramatic irony?
options: When the audience knows something a character does not
When a character says the opposite of what they mean
When a play has a sad ending
questions.answer: When the audience knows something a character does not
questions.hint: Think about the gap between what the audience knows and what a character knows.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What is a soliloquy?
options: A speech in which a character alone on stage speaks their thoughts aloud
A short remark to the audience that others cannot hear
A song at the end of a scene
questions.answer: A speech in which a character alone on stage speaks their thoughts aloud
questions.hint: The word comes from Latin 'solus', meaning alone.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What is an aside?
options: A brief remark to the audience that other characters on stage do not hear
A long speech by a character alone
questions.answer: A brief remark to the audience that other characters on stage do not hear
questions.hint: It is shorter than a soliloquy and other characters are present.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What is a monologue?
options: A long speech by one character, which others on stage may hear
The final line of a play
questions.answer: A long speech by one character, which others on stage may hear
questions.hint: 'Mono' means one.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: A stage direction reads: '(She slams the door and the lights snap to black.)' What does this most suggest?
options: A sudden, dramatic end to the scene
questions.answer: A sudden, dramatic end to the scene
questions.hint: Think about the effect of 'slams' and 'snap'.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: In a play, the audience has seen a character hide a stolen letter. Another character says, 'I trust you completely.' What technique is being used?
questions.hint: The audience knows more than the speaker.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Why is a play script mainly written in dialogue rather than description?
options: Because it is meant to be performed and heard
Because it is shorter to print
questions.answer: Because it is meant to be performed and heard
questions.hint: Think about how an audience experiences a play.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What does the term 'tension' mean in drama?
options: A feeling of suspense or anxiety the audience experiences
The number of actors on stage
questions.answer: A feeling of suspense or anxiety the audience experiences
questions.hint: It keeps the audience on the edge of their seats.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Which is the most likely effect of dramatic irony on an audience?
options: It builds tension as they wait for the truth to come out
It makes the audience forget the plot
questions.answer: It builds tension as they wait for the truth to come out
questions.hint: Think about how it feels to know a secret that a character does not.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Stage directions that describe a character 'nervously twisting a ring' mainly help to show what?
questions.hint: Actions can reveal emotions without words.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Explain how a playwright can use stage directions to create atmosphere at the start of a scene.
questions.hint: Think about lighting, sound, setting and how characters move or are positioned.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Analyse how dramatic irony can make an audience feel sympathy for a character.
questions.hint: Consider how it feels to watch a character trust someone or walk into danger without knowing what we know.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Explain why it is important to think about performance when analysing a play, rather than treating it only as a text to read.
questions.hint: Consider tone of voice, movement, pauses, staging and the live audience.
